titulo: Semantic HTML and a well-labeled form: the interface every agent already reads
lead: Before any tool for agents, there is an interface they all already read: HTML. A label tied to its field, a real button, a main region, a heading, a language, and alt text. It is stable, it works for screen readers and for agents, and it does not depend on an experimental browser. In this lesson you fix the sample page until the check comes back at zero.
objetivo: fix the labels, button, regions, and alt text until arvore.mjs finds no problems in your copy of the page.

aprende.t: Six fixes the agent feels right away
Bring the same fix to your own site

hero_alt: A bike shop tool wall, each tool in its own outline with a blank label, and a monitor in the corner.

secoes.titulo: Six fixes, from the old page to the new one
secoes.sub: Click each one. All of them show up in the arvore.mjs check.

nos.detalhe: Each field gets a <label for="id">. The name becomes the label text, which doesn't disappear when the person types. Placeholder stays as a hint, never as the name.
An action is a <button type="submit"> inside a <form>. It works with the keyboard, shows up as button in the tree, and submits the form without extra JavaScript.
<main> marks the main content and an <h1> says what the page is about. The agent separates the task from the menu and the footer.
<html lang="pt-BR"> says what language the text is in. Screen readers pronounce it correctly; reading tools know what they are reading.
Every with content gets alt text that describes what it shows. A decorative image gets alt="" and disappears from the tree.
The form's response goes in an <output role="status">. The agent (and the screen reader) finds the result by its role, without searching for text on the screen.

secoes.legenda: Native element first: button, label, main. ARIA only where HTML doesn't have the right element.

secoes.sub: The snippet that changed from antes.html to depois.html. The form works on its own, for people and for any agent that operates the screen.

  - heading "Agendar revisão" [level=1]
  - img "Bicicleta na bancada da oficina"

  - text: Seu nome
  - textbox "Seu nome"
  - text: Serviço
  - combobox "Serviço":
    - option "Escolha" [selected]
    - option "Revisão básica"
    - option "Revisão completa"
  - text: Data
  - textbox "Data"
  - button "Agendar"
  - status
## conferência · http://127.0.0.1:PORTA/depois.html
problemas: 0
saída: 0

Now everything has a role and a name: heading, img with a description, the three fields, the button "Agendar", and the status for the response. The tree grew from 182 to 415 bytes, and the check comes back at zero.

abas.rot: Common mistake: fixing it with ARIA on a div
abas.html: Putting role="button" and aria-label on the clickable div makes the tree show a button, but it doesn't get keyboard focus or fire on Enter without more JavaScript, and it doesn't submit the form. arvore.mjs keeps flagging <div> clicável que não é botão, on purpose: swap it for the button.

secoes.sub: Copy antes.html to a folder of your own and run the check: 10 problems. Then edit the copy until it hits zero. arvore.mjs accepts the path to any .html.

perguntas.p: What is the right way to give a form text field a name?
opcoes: A label element tied to the field with for
A placeholder with the field name inside it
A title attribute on the input with the name
Bold text right above the field
perguntas.explica: The label tied with for becomes the accessible name and stays visible. A placeholder disappears when you type, and loose text above the field isn't tied to it.

perguntas.p: Why swap the clickable div for a button, instead of putting role="button" on the div?
opcoes: Because role="button" is forbidden by the WebMCP spec
Because the div makes the page much slower on a phone
Because the agent only reads elements that have their own id
Because button already comes with focus, keyboard, and submit
perguntas.explica: Native element first: button gets focus, fires with Enter, and submits the form. The role only changes what the tree shows; you'd have to program the rest.

perguntas.p: The form's response appears in some random div. What changes when you use <output role="status">?
opcoes: Nothing for the agent; it only changes the text color on screen
The agent finds the result by the status role
The form becomes a registered WebMCP tool
The result goes to the site's MCP server
perguntas.explica: status is an accessibility tree role: the agent reads there what happened after the click. It has nothing to do with WebMCP; it's stable HTML.

perguntas.p: Does this HTML fix depend on an origin trial or a flag in Chrome?
opcoes: Yes, it only works with the published origin trial token
Yes, it needs the enable-webmcp-testing flag turned on
No: it's stable HTML, read by agents
Only in Edge 150, which has the origin trial open
perguntas.explica: Label, button, regions, and alt are plain old HTML. That's the stable base; WebMCP is the experimental part.

itens.texto: label, button, main and h1, lang, alt, and status.
The right element before ARIA; ARIA doesn't submit a form.
arvore.mjs tells you what's missing, on your copy and on your site.
